# Dual Suspension to Monoshock Conversion: A Practical Guide

Converting a dual suspension motorcycle to a monoshock setup is a significant mechanical undertaking that goes far beyond a simple bolt swap. While online galleries show successful conversions, particularly on platforms like the Bajaj Discover 135, the engineering reality involves replacing the entire rear swingarm architecture or finding a specific sub-frame that accepts a single shock absorber. The core challenge isn't just removing the existing components; it is ensuring the new geometry maintains proper chain alignment, brake clearance, and rider ergonomics without compromising structural integrity.

To execute this modification on a Discover 135, you must first assess the swingarm itself. Most stock dual-suspension bikes feature a swingarm designed with two pivot points for the rear shock mounts. A monoshock requires a single pivot point located higher up, typically near the engine casing or within a specific sub-frame bracket. If your bike uses a standard tubular steel swingarm common to many 135cc models, you generally cannot mount a monoshock directly onto the existing arm. You will likely need to source a complete rear end kit that includes a sub-frame specifically cast or welded to accept a monoshock link.

The process begins with stripping the rear section. This involves removing the seat unit, the rear sub-frame (if separate), and the exhaust system if it clashes with new mounting points. You must disconnect the rear brake lines and electrical wiring for the tail light and turn signals. These are critical steps often overlooked; simply cutting wires is a recipe for expensive electrical failures later. Once the old shock absorbers and linkage arms are removed, inspect the frame rails for stress cracks or weld fatigue, especially around the rear axle mounting points.

Installing the new monoshock assembly requires precise alignment. The primary technical decision here is determining the correct pivot location. If you opt for a sub-frame conversion, you must ensure the new bracket aligns perfectly with the swingarm's existing pivot holes or that the swingarm itself is drilled and re-tapped to match the new mounting geometry. Misalignment here leads to "chain growth" issues where the chain rubs against the frame or creates excessive tension on one side of the drivetrain.

You will also need to address the brake disc clearance. Monoshock setups often raise the rear axle slightly compared to dual suspension geometries. If your brake caliper is mounted directly to the swingarm, you may find it hitting the new shock mount or the sub-frame extension. In such cases, you must verify whether a new caliper bracket or an offset adapter plate is required to maintain the correct braking distance from the disc.

Another consideration is the rear suspension spring preload and damping. The original dual-shock setup distributes load across two units; moving to one shock concentrates that force on a single unit. You must select a shock absorber with a spring rate capable of handling the bike's weight plus any additional load from cargo or passengers without bottoming out excessively.

Finally, do not underestimate the labor involved in routing the exhaust and the electrical harness around the new bulkier sub-frame components. Many conversion kits available for 135cc bikes are sold as "drop-in" replacements, but they often require custom bending of the muffler or trimming of wire looms to fit within the frame rails without snagging on moving parts.

If you decide to proceed with this modification, ensure you have access to a workshop equipped for heavy fabrication and alignment checks. The complexity of the job means that a generic online tutorial is rarely sufficient; specific diagrams for your exact Discover 135 model year are essential to avoid fitting errors.
